title: Changing to the eigenvector basis
objectives: Diagonalise a matrix and use it to compute powers quickly.
Read a matrix as two stretches in its eigenvector basis.

screens.title: A grid made of eigenvectors
screens.prose: $\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ triples $\mathbf{x}_1 = (1, 1)$ and keeps $\mathbf{x}_2 = (1, -1)$. The grid is built from these two. $\mathbf{u} = (3, 1)$ is 2 steps along $\mathbf{x}_1$ and 1 step along $\mathbf{x}_2$.
screens.question: Drag the head of $\mathbf{w}$ to $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{u}$.

hints.text: Work in grid steps: what happens to the 2 steps along $\mathbf{x}_1$, and to the 1 step along $\mathbf{x}_2$?
The 2 steps along $\mathbf{x}_1$ become 6. The step along $\mathbf{x}_2$ stays 1.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count grid steps: triple the $\mathbf{x}_1$ steps, keep the $\mathbf{x}_2$ step.

byKey.triple-u: You tripled all of $\mathbf{u}$. Only the $\mathbf{x}_1$ part is tripled; the $\mathbf{x}_2$ part stays.
byKey.coords: $(6, 1)$ are the grid steps of $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{u}$, not its coordinates. Walk 6 along $\mathbf{x}_1$, then 1 along $\mathbf{x}_2$.
byKey.swapped: You tripled the $\mathbf{x}_2$ step. $\mathbf{A}$ triples $\mathbf{x}_1 = (1, 1)$ and keeps $\mathbf{x}_2$.

explain.text: In grid steps $\mathbf{u}$ is $(2, 1)$ and $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{u}$ is $(6, 1)$: only the $\mathbf{x}_1$ count changes. Converting back gives $6(1, 1) + (1, -1) = (7, 5)$. Check directly: $\mathbf{A}(3, 1) = (6 + 1, 3 + 2) = (7, 5)$.

screens.prose: The grid steps are the **eigen-coordinates** $(c_1, c_2)$: $\mathbf{u} = c_1\mathbf{x}_1 + c_2\mathbf{x}_2$. Drag $\mathbf{u}$ and compare its eigen-coordinates with those of $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{u}$ in the caption.
screens.question: In eigen-coordinates, what does $\mathbf{A}$ do to $(c_1, c_2)$?

options.why: Only the $\mathbf{x}_1$ count is tripled. At $\mathbf{u} = (2, 0)$ the caption reads $(1, 1)$ then $(3, 1)$, not $(3, 3)$.
That is $\mathbf{A}$ in ordinary coordinates. In eigen-coordinates the mixing disappears.
The tripled direction is $\mathbf{x}_1 = (1, 1)$, which is the first coordinate.

feedback.correct: In eigen-coordinates $\mathbf{A}$ is just two stretches: by 3 and by 1.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read both pairs in the caption for a few positions of $\mathbf{u}$.

explain.text: Each count is multiplied by its own eigenvalue and nothing mixes. In the eigenbasis, $\mathbf{A}$ is the diagonal matrix $\begin{pmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$.

screens.title: Diagonalisation
screens.prose: Read $\mathbf{A}$ as three moves. $\mathbf{X}^{-1}$ turns $\mathbf{u}$ into eigen-coordinates, $\boldsymbol{\Lambda}$ stretches them, and $\mathbf{X}$ turns them back. $\mathbf{X}$ holds the eigenvectors as columns, and $\boldsymbol{\Lambda}$ the eigenvalues in the same order. This is **diagonalisation**: $\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{X}^{-1}$.
screens.question: Fill in $\mathbf{X}^{-1}$.

hints.text: For a $2 \times 2$ inverse, swap the diagonal, negate the off-diagonal, and divide by the determinant.
$\frac{1}{-2}\begin{pmatrix} -1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0.5 & 0.5 \\ 0.5 & -0.5 \end{pmatrix}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the $2 \times 2$ inverse with $\det\mathbf{X} = -2$.

byKey.r1c2: Bottom right: the swapped entry is 1, and $1 / (-2) = -0.5$.

explain.text: $\det\mathbf{X} = -2$, so $\mathbf{X}^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} 0.5 & 0.5 \\ 0.5 & -0.5 \end{pmatrix}$. Its rows give the eigen-coordinates you watched: $c_1 = (x + y)/2$ and $c_2 = (x - y)/2$.

screens.prose: Square it: $\mathbf{A}^2 = \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{X}^{-1}\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{X}^{-1}$. The middle $\mathbf{X}^{-1}\mathbf{X}$ is $\mathbf{I}$, so $\mathbf{A}^2 = \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^2\mathbf{X}^{-1}$. Squaring a diagonal matrix squares its entries.
screens.question: Multiply out the top row of $\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^2\mathbf{X}^{-1}$.

hints.text: Do $\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^2$ first: it scales column 1 of $\mathbf{X}$ by 9.
Row 1 of $\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^2$ is $(9, 1)$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Scale the columns of $\mathbf{X}$ by 9 and 1, then multiply by $\mathbf{X}^{-1}$.

explain.text: Row 1 of $\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^2$ is $(9, 1)$, and $(9, 1)\mathbf{X}^{-1} = (5, 4)$. Directly, row 1 of $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{A}$ is $(4 + 1, 2 + 2) = (5, 4)$. The two routes agree.

screens.prose: Now $\mathbf{A}^{10}$. Multiplying directly takes nine matrix products. The eigen route needs only $3^{10} = 59049$ and $1^{10} = 1$, then one sandwich.
screens.question: What is the top row of $\mathbf{A}^{10}$?

hints.text: Same pattern as the last screen, with 59049 in place of 9.
Row 1 of $\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{10}$ is $(59049, 1)$.

explain.text: In general $\mathbf{A}^k = \frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix} 3^k + 1 & 3^k - 1 \\ 3^k - 1 & 3^k + 1 \end{pmatrix}$. For $k = 10$ that gives 29525 and 29524, the same as nine direct products. The work hardly grows with $k$.

screens.prose: The shear $\mathbf{S} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ has $\lambda = 1$ twice, and every eigenvector lies along $(1, 0)$. Try to build $\mathbf{X}$ from two of its eigenvectors.
screens.question: Why can $\mathbf{S}$ not be diagonalised?

options.text: Its eigenvectors all lie on one line, so no invertible $\mathbf{X}$ exists
A repeated eigenvalue can never be diagonalised
options.why: $2\mathbf{I}$ has $\lambda = 2$ twice and is already diagonal. A repeat is fine when there are two independent eigenvectors.
$\mathbf{S} - \mathbf{I}$ sends $(1, 0)$ to $\mathbf{0}$, so $\lambda = 1$ is an eigenvalue.

options.text: $\boldsymbol{\Lambda}$ would need a 0 on its diagonal
options.why: $\boldsymbol{\Lambda} = \mathbf{I}$ here, with no zero. The block is $\mathbf{X}$, not $\boldsymbol{\Lambda}$.

hints.text: What is $\det\mathbf{X}$ for the $\mathbf{X}$ shown?
Both columns of $\mathbf{X}$ lie along $(1, 0)$.
$\det\mathbf{X} = 0$, so $\mathbf{X}^{-1}$ does not exist. With only one eigen-direction there is no second column to choose.

feedback.correct: Two eigenvectors on one line make $\det\mathbf{X} = 0$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check whether the $\mathbf{X}$ shown can be inverted.

byKey.repeat: You blamed the repeated eigenvalue. $2\mathbf{I}$ repeats $\lambda = 2$ yet has two eigen-directions.

explain.text: A $2 \times 2$ matrix needs two independent eigenvectors to fill $\mathbf{X}$. The shear has only one direction, so any $\mathbf{X}$ built from its eigenvectors has $\det\mathbf{X} = 0$. Such a matrix is called defective.

screens.prose: $\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvalue 5 with $(1, 1)$ and eigenvalue 2 with $(1, -2)$. So $\mathbf{X} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -2 \end{pmatrix}$.
screens.question: Which product gives back $\mathbf{A}$?

options.why: You put 2 first, but column 1 of $\mathbf{X}$ is $(1, 1)$, whose eigenvalue is 5. This product is $\begin{pmatrix} 3 & -1 \\ -2 & 4 \end{pmatrix}$.
You reversed the outer factors. That product is $\begin{pmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ 1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$, the transpose of $\mathbf{A}$ here.
$\boldsymbol{\Lambda}$ is $\mathbf{A}$ in eigen-coordinates. In ordinary coordinates you must convert in and out.

hints.text: The right-most factor acts first. It should turn $\mathbf{u}$ into eigen-coordinates.
Column $i$ of $\mathbf{X}$ must sit with the $i$-th diagonal entry of $\boldsymbol{\Lambda}$.
$\mathbf{X}^{-1}$ first, then $\mathrm{diag}(5, 2)$ in column order, then $\mathbf{X}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Match the eigenvalue order to the columns of $\mathbf{X}$, and let $\mathbf{X}^{-1}$ act first.

byKey.order: You ordered the eigenvalues differently from the columns. Each $\lambda_i$ must sit under its own eigenvector $\mathbf{x}_i$.
byKey.flip: You wrote $\mathbf{X}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{X}$. That converts the wrong way round.

explain.text: $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}$ holds column by column only when $\lambda_i$ sits under $\mathbf{x}_i$. Then multiplying on the right by $\mathbf{X}^{-1}$ gives $\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{X}^{-1}$. Swapping either the order or the sides gives a different matrix.

screens.prose: Stack the eigenvector equations side by side. Column $i$ of $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{X}$ is $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}_i$, and column $i$ of $\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}$ is $\lambda_i\mathbf{x}_i$. $$\mathbf{A}\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\Lambda} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \mathbf{A} = \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{X}^{-1},$$ whenever $\mathbf{X}$ is invertible.
screens.question: What is column 2 of $\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}$?

options.why: Column 2 of $\boldsymbol{\Lambda}$ has $\lambda_2$ in row 2 and 0 elsewhere, so it picks $\lambda_2$.
$\mathbf{X}$ times column 2 of $\boldsymbol{\Lambda}$ takes $\lambda_2$ copies of column 2 of $\mathbf{X}$, which is $\mathbf{x}_2$.
$\boldsymbol{\Lambda}$ scales each column of $\mathbf{X}$ by its eigenvalue.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply $\mathbf{X}$ by column 2 of $\boldsymbol{\Lambda}$, which is $(0, \lambda_2)$.

explain.text: $\mathbf{X}(0, \lambda_2) = \lambda_2\mathbf{x}_2$. So $\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}$ has columns $\lambda_1\mathbf{x}_1$ and $\lambda_2\mathbf{x}_2$, matching $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}_1$ and $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}_2$.

screens.prose: You found $\mathbf{A}^2$ and $\mathbf{A}^{10}$ by powering only $\boldsymbol{\Lambda}$. Now justify it for any power $k$.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: $\mathbf{A}^k = \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^k\mathbf{X}^{-1}$, since each extra factor cancels one more pair
$\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^k = \mathrm{diag}(\lambda_1^k, \lambda_2^k)$, since a diagonal matrix powers entry by entry

hints.text: Start with two copies of $\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{X}^{-1}$ side by side.
The inner $\mathbf{X}^{-1}\mathbf{X}$ is what disappears.
Write $\mathbf{A}^2$, regroup, cancel to $\mathbf{I}$, extend to $k$, then power the diagonal.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each line should follow from the one before.

byKey.cancel: You need the regrouping first, so that $\mathbf{X}^{-1}\mathbf{X}$ sits together.
byKey.k: The general $k$ comes after you have seen one pair cancel.

explain.text: Between neighbouring copies, $\mathbf{X}^{-1}\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{I}$ drops out, so $k$ copies leave $\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^k\mathbf{X}^{-1}$. With your matrix, $\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{10} = \mathrm{diag}(59049, 1)$.

screens.title: Ten years of credit migration
screens.prose: A loan is rated Good or Bad each year. Column $j$ of $\mathbf{P} = \begin{pmatrix} 0.95 & 0.1 \\ 0.05 & 0.9 \end{pmatrix}$ gives next year's chances from state $j$. $\mathbf{P}$ has eigenvalue 1 with $(2, 1)$ and eigenvalue 0.85 with $(1, -1)$.
screens.question: What is the chance that a Good loan is Bad after 10 years?

widget.label: Chance Good to Bad in 10 years

hints.text: You need the entry in row Bad, column Good of $\mathbf{P}^{10}$.
Row 2 of $\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{10}$ is $(1, -0.1969)$.
Times column 1 of $\mathbf{X}^{-1}$, $(\tfrac{1}{3}, \tfrac{1}{3})$: $\tfrac{1}{3} - \tfrac{0.1969}{3} \approx 0.2677$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the (Bad, Good) entry of $\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{10}\mathbf{X}^{-1}$.

byKey.add: You added the yearly 5% ten times. Chances do not add across years, and Bad loans can recover.
byKey.no-cure: $1 - 0.95^{10}$ assumes a loan that turns Bad stays Bad. $\mathbf{P}$ lets 10% recover each year.
byKey.limit: $\tfrac{1}{3}$ is the long-run share, reached as $k$ grows. After 10 years $0.85^{10}$ has not yet died away.
byKey.one-year: 0.05 is the chance for one year. You need ten.

explain.text: $\mathbf{P}^{10}$ has (Bad, Good) entry $\tfrac{1}{3}(1 - 0.85^{10}) = \tfrac{1}{3}(1 - 0.1969) \approx 0.268$. As $k$ grows, $0.85^k \to 0$ and the entry tends to $\tfrac{1}{3}$. Lesson 4 is about that limit.

ideas: In eigen-coordinates a diagonalisable matrix is just stretches: $(c_1, c_2) \mapsto (\lambda_1 c_1, \lambda_2 c_2)$.
Put the eigenvectors in the columns of $\mathbf{X}$ and the eigenvalues, in the same order, in $\boldsymbol{\Lambda}$: $\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{X}^{-1}$.
Powers come cheap: $\mathbf{A}^k = \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^k\mathbf{X}^{-1}$. A matrix with too few independent eigenvectors, like a shear, cannot be diagonalised.

formula.name: Diagonalisation
formula.note: $\mathbf{X}^{-1}$ acts first: into eigen-coordinates, stretch, and back.

summary.trap: $\boldsymbol{\Lambda}$ must list the eigenvalues in the order of the columns of $\mathbf{X}$, and the product is $\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{X}^{-1}$, not $\mathbf{X}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{X}$.

quiz.prose: $\mathbf{A}$ has eigenvalue 2 with $(1, 0)$ and eigenvalue 3 with $(1, 1)$. We take $\mathbf{X} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$.
quiz.question: Which $\boldsymbol{\Lambda}$ makes $\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{X}^{-1}$?

options.why: Column 1 of $\mathbf{X}$ is $(1, 0)$, whose eigenvalue is 2. The order must match.
That is $\mathbf{X}$ itself. $\boldsymbol{\Lambda}$ is diagonal and holds the eigenvalues.

feedback.correct: $\mathrm{diag}(2, 3)$, in the order of the columns of $\mathbf{X}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Match each eigenvalue to its column.

explain.text: Column 1 of $\mathbf{X}$ is $(1, 0)$, which goes with 2, and column 2 is $(1, 1)$, which goes with 3. So $\boldsymbol{\Lambda} = \mathrm{diag}(2, 3)$.

options.why: You multiplied by 4. $\mathbf{A}^4 = \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^4\mathbf{X}^{-1}$ raises each eigenvalue to the fourth power.
$(-1)^4 = 1$: an even power removes the sign.
$\mathbf{A}^4$ has the same eigenvectors, but its eigenvalues are powered.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Power each diagonal entry of $\boldsymbol{\Lambda}$.

explain.text: $\mathbf{A}^4 = \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^4\mathbf{X}^{-1}$ and $\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^4 = \mathrm{diag}(16, 1)$. The eigenvectors stay the same.

quiz.question: What is the top-left entry of $\mathbf{A}^3$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Row 1 of $\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^3$ is $(64, 8)$; then use $\mathbf{X}^{-1}$.

byKey.entry: You cubed the entry 3. Matrix powers do not work entry by entry.
byKey.sum: $216 = 6^3$ cubes the sum of the eigenvalues. Cube each one: 64 and 8.

explain.text: Row 1 of $\mathbf{X}\,\mathrm{diag}(64, 8)$ is $(64, 8)$, and column 1 of $\mathbf{X}^{-1}$ is $(0.5, 0.5)$. So the entry is $32 + 4 = 36$. Direct: $\mathbf{A}^2$ has top row $(10, 6)$, and $10 \cdot 3 + 6 \cdot 1 = 36$.

quiz.prose: One of these matrices cannot be diagonalised.
quiz.question: Which one?

options.why: It repeats 4, but every vector is an eigenvector. It is already diagonal.
Its eigenvalues 4 and 3 differ, so it has two independent eigenvectors.
Eigenvalues 1 and $-1$, with $(1, 1)$ and $(1, -1)$: two directions.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for a repeated eigenvalue with a single eigen-direction.

explain.text: For $\begin{pmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 0 & 4 \end{pmatrix}$, $\mathbf{A} - 4\mathbf{I}$ has row $(0, 1)$, forcing $v_2 = 0$. One direction cannot fill a $2 \times 2$ $\mathbf{X}$.
